attempt: Water that appears half an hour after a load and smells foul is drain water getting back into the tub, not fresh water: the usual causes are a drain hose set too low (water siphons back), a failed check valve or drain-pump seal, or a leaking door bellow (which would give fresh water). Check the drain hose height against the manual (it must rise to the recommended height before turning down), run a drain-only cycle and watch for seep-back, and inspect the bellows. Foul smell means the drain side; clean-smelling water means the door seal.
thread_resolution: drain water siphoning back through the low drain run to the utility sink (top answer, score 8); the accepted answer names the clogged front filter instead
grade_reason: The attempt's primary hypothesis is the thread's top-voted cause (drain water backing up, drain-hose height) and its actions (drain-only cycle, check the drain path) cover the accepted answer's class as well.

attempt: Stuck full of water before the rinse cycle, fixable only by finding a knob sweet spot, points to an intermittent electrical contact in the timer/cycle switch or its knob, or a lid switch the machine does not see. Drain the tub first (emergency drain or a hose lowered to floor level), then check the lid switch for a click. If the machine only advances when the knob is wiggled, the timer or the knob's wiring pads are the fault; on an Ultimate Care II the timer is the common wear item for exactly this symptom.
thread_resolution: a dirty or worn timer-switch — the 'sweet spot' is worn timer contacts or gears (top answer, score 4); several lower answers name the lid/door switch
grade_reason: The attempt names the timer/cycle switch first and the lid switch second, matching both of the thread's cause classes, with the drain-the-tub action the thread also gives.

attempt: Slow dispenser flow immediately after a filter change is usually an air lock in the filter housing, a filter that was not flushed, a partially closed saddle valve, or a wrong/clogged filter. Dispense two to three gallons to clear air, confirm the saddle valve is fully open, and check the seat seal for the leak seen at the housing. If flow stays slow after several gallons, the filter is clogged or the wrong part for that GE model.
thread_resolution: air in the system: a new filter is full of air; bleed it by dispensing or by refilling the filter in the sink (top answer, score 5)
grade_reason: The attempt's first hypothesis is an air lock and its first action is to dispense two to three gallons — the thread's resolution, verbatim.

attempt: A rotting-garbage smell with standing water under the filter assembly means debris in the sump or a partially blocked drain: a clean filter does not clean the sump strainer or the drain. Remove the lower filter and sump cover, clear the strainer and the drain of food, check the drain hose for a clog, and run a hot empty cycle with a dishwasher cleaner. If the standing water is deep rather than the usual shallow puddle, the drain pump or its check valve is the fault.
thread_resolution: a bleach/cleaner cycle for a modern water-saving machine, plus a drain-path check if standing water persists (accepted answer, score 5); other answers name the sump, the drain-hose loop and sewer gases
grade_reason: The attempt names the sump/drain class and prescribes the hot empty cycle with a dishwasher cleaner — the accepted answer's action — with the drain-hose check the other answers add.

attempt: A washer that trips a GFCI mid-cycle has a ground fault: most often water from a leaking hose, pump seal, or inlet valve reaching a live part, or (on heated models) a cracked heating element grounding through the water. Dry the machine, check hoses and the pump area for leaks, and briefly test on a non-GFCI outlet to confirm the fault is in the machine rather than the outlet. Do not bypass the GFCI; a machine that trips it is unsafe until the leak is found.
thread_resolution: isolate the three possibilities first — the machine, the downstream wiring, or the GFCI outlet itself — by swapping the outlet (accepted answer, score 2); a leaking pump and starved inlet screens appear in lower answers
grade_reason: The attempt names machine-side ground faults and includes the thread's key first action: test on another outlet to isolate the machine from the outlet.

attempt: The black film on the axle is degraded lubricant or the nylon roller surface stripping, and these rollers are plain nylon bushings that are not meant to hold grease: oil and grease migrate and gum the bushing. Clean the axles and rollers of all old lubricant, dry thoroughly, and run them dry (nylon is self-lubricating) or with a silicone lubricant sparingly. Replace any roller with a flat spot or a crack. If the film reappears, the roller material itself is failing and the rollers should be replaced, not re-lubricated.
thread_resolution: grease or nothing beats oil here; the black film is lubricant plus dust; use a dry lubricant (spray Teflon or graphite) — accepted answer, score 8
grade_reason: The attempt agrees on the cause (degraded lubricant or surface wear), agrees oil/grease is the wrong choice, and prescribes cleaning plus dry lubrication — the thread's resolution. The wax-motor/solenoid naming in the attempt is the same component class the thread names.

attempt: Condensation that drips in a long, upward vent run in hot humid weather is the exhaust cooling and condensing in the attic section, then running back. Insulate the vent where it passes through the attic, keep the run as short and straight as the installation allows, and make sure the roof cap has a working damper. A crushed or lint-choked duct makes it worse. If the dryer is gas, have the installation checked for combustion safety before continuing to use it.
thread_resolution: check the vent's exit flap first — outside air is coming in (accepted answer, score 14); the 25-foot run with two elbows may exceed the vent length limit (score 6), and moist air condensing in the vent is the mechanism (score 1)
grade_reason: The attempt names the condensation mechanism, the vent-length problem, and the damper/flap check — all three of the thread's answers — with insulation and a shorter run as the actions.

attempt: After a fridge is left open all day, a cold freezer with a warm fridge points to cold air not reaching the fridge: the evaporator fan (it only runs in some cycles), a blocked vent between the compartments, or a defrost problem — or it may simply need 24 hours to recover. Listen for the fan whenever the compressor runs; if it never runs while the freezer is cold, the fan or its damper is the fault. Clear the vent and give it overnight before replacing anything.
thread_resolution: the vent from freezer to fridge has frozen over with ice — warm the freezer to melt it (top answer, score 15); the evaporator fan (score 2) and the door alignment (score 3) also appear
grade_reason: The attempt's two named causes are the thread's top two mechanisms (blocked/frozen vent, evaporator fan), with the overnight-wait and fan-listen actions the thread gives.

attempt: Orange flames on every gas appliance at once, with normal measured pressure, is a supply-side problem, not an appliance problem: pressure can be right while the gas itself is wrong, or a regulator is still faulty, or air is being drawn into the line. Stop using the appliances (soot means incomplete combustion and a CO risk) and ask the gas company specifically for a gas-quality analysis, a regulator inspection, and a leak-down test with the system pressurized and isolated. Appliance-level fixes cannot address a problem every appliance shares.
thread_resolution: a supply-side problem: contamination or water in the line (accepted answer, score 9); the gas-company technician's own resolution for a similar report was a household humidifier (score 5)
grade_reason: The attempt correctly classifies the row vendor-side and routes to the gas company for a gas-quality analysis and regulator inspection — the accepted answer's class. The humidifier cause is not named.

attempt: The beeper works from the buttons but the timer-end signal does not sound, so the speaker is good and the fault is in the end-of-cycle signal path: a control setting (many Whirlpool ovens have a signal/sound on-off option) or the timer buzzer circuit. Check the manual for a sound or signal setting first, then reset the control (breaker off for one to two minutes). If the setting is on and the reset does not restore the end-of-cycle beep, the buzzer or its drive on the control board has failed.
thread_resolution: the beeper was simply turned off: press and hold COOK TIME for five seconds to turn tones on (accepted answer, score 2, from the Owner Manual); a breaker reset also worked for another user
grade_reason: The attempt's first hypothesis is the sound setting and its first action is the manual check, followed by the control reset — the thread's two resolutions in order.

attempt: Water heard under the drum after the spin cycle, with a mildew smell, is incomplete draining: a clogged drain pump, a kinked drain hose, or a too-low standpipe. If the water is fresh-smelling instead, a leaking inlet valve dribbles water in continuously while the machine does not fully drain. Check the drain hose for clogs and the standpipe height, run a drain-only cycle and watch the pump, and treat the smell with a cleaner once the drain is clear.
thread_resolution: the water under the drum is supposed to be there; the smell is the rubber lining — bleach wash and prop the door open (top answer, score 1); a pinched drain hose appears only in a comment
grade_reason: The attempt's primary hypothesis (incomplete draining) is contradicted by the thread's top answer, and its resolution (mildew maintenance, ventilation) is absent. The drain-hose check the attempt does name matches a comment, not an answer.

attempt: Two dishwashers in a row that do not drain, with the old one's hose and trap already cleaned, points to the household drain, not the machines: a clogged shared drain line, a blocked air gap, or a drain hose without the required high loop (which lets the machine siphon). Run the drain hose into a bucket: if the machine pumps freely into the bucket, the machine is fine and the shared drain line or air gap is the blockage; if it does not pump, the pump or its check valve is the fault.
thread_resolution: the household drain: a clogged flexible drain hose (top answers, score 4 x2 — blow into the hose to test; the crawlspace run can freeze), and the wrong hose entirely (score 1)
grade_reason: The attempt names the drain-side class the thread converges on and prescribes the same isolation test (run the hose into a bucket), which is the thread's blow-into-the-hose test.

attempt: White filaments in fridge water right after a filter change are usually mineral sediment stirred up by the new filter's first flow, or carbon fines from a filter that was not flushed. Run two to four gallons through the dispenser to flush it. If the filaments persist after flushing, the supply lines are shedding scale (common after plumbing work) and the line should be flushed at the supply; a sediment filter at the supply is the durable fix. White and hard means scale; black means carbon fines.
thread_resolution: chloramine in the water supply attacks the molded plastic reservoir, releasing white flakes — the filter is not the cause and the reservoir must be replaced (top answer, score 2)
grade_reason: The attempt names the wrong class (mineral sediment, carbon fines) where the thread converges on the reservoir plastic, and its resolution (replace the reservoir / remove the filter) is absent. Flushing is shared, but the fault class is not.

attempt: Out-of-balance with the lightest loads, banging, and repeated repositioning on a front-loader points to worn suspension shocks, tub bearings, or a leveling problem: worn shocks let the tub slam at spin even with small loads. Re-level the machine first (every foot should resist rocking with the door open), confirm no shipping bolts remain, and push the tub: it should resist, not swing. If leveling does not fix it, the shock absorbers or bearings need replacement; the service manual's balance test will confirm which.
thread_resolution: the suspension rods (accepted answer, score 1: primary suspicion, with leveling re-checked); the rod's elastomer damper disintegrates and the rods must be replaced as a set (score 0); the asker's service tech quoted the drum bearing/axle at half a new machine
grade_reason: The attempt names worn suspension and leveling first — the thread's primary suspicion — then the bearings, matching the asker's own narrowed diagnosis and the follow-up comment.

attempt: Ice that builds in the vent between freezer and fridge until it blocks airflow is the defrost system not clearing the evaporator, or humid air leaking past a door gasket. Defrost the vent fully (low heat, carefully, since the structure is foam), then check the freezer gasket with a dollar-bill test. If ice returns within days of a full defrost, the defrost heater, defrost thermostat, or defrost timer is the fault; if it returns slowly over weeks, the gasket is the leak.
thread_resolution: the automatic defroster is out (check the defrost heater, limit switch, or timer) or a badly closing door seal is letting humid air in (both score 1)
grade_reason: The attempt names both causes with the same tests: a full defrost, then the gasket check, then the defrost components if the ice returns quickly — the thread's differential, in order.

attempt: A spin-cycle noise that starts when the water is gone, without grinding or shaking, is most consistent with worn tub bearings or a worn spin tube: bearing noise is load-dependent and loudest when the empty tub spins fast. Open the cabinet and spin the tub by hand: a rumble that worsens with speed is the bearing; also inspect the belt and pulley for wear. If it is the bearings, continued use wears the spin tube and outer tub, so repair now rather than later.
thread_resolution: check the leveling first (cheap fix); if it is the bearings the repair is expensive and often means replacing the machine; continuing to run it damages the drum and shaft (top answers, score 2 x2)
grade_reason: The attempt names the bearing class the thread and the asker's hypothesis converge on, answers the question asked (consequences of continued use: spin-tube and outer-tub wear), and gives the by-hand spin test the thread's answers imply.

attempt: An intermittent breaker trip on a ten-year-old fridge in hot weather is most often the compressor start relay or overload (tripping on start, especially in heat), or a grounded winding from a damp connection after defrost. Watch the timing: a trip within seconds of the compressor starting points to the start relay; a trip after running points to the compressor or a grounded winding. Clean the condenser coils; an electrician can megger the winding to ground.
thread_resolution: swap the fridge's breaker with another of the same rating to test whether the breaker has de-rated itself — the cheapest, fastest first test (top answer, score 2)
grade_reason: The attempt's cause class (compressor start relay, grounded winding) does not include the thread's top answer — a failing breaker — and none of the attempt's actions would find it. The question asked what to look at FIRST; the thread says the breaker.

attempt: Sides that are hot to 105F with loud running, when the machine used to run cool and quiet, is a change, and the technician's 'that is how it works' only holds for a clean machine: the usual cause is clogged condenser coils, then a failed condenser fan, then a compressor working too hard (low charge or wear). Clean the coils first and listen for the condenser fan; if coils and fan are clean and it still runs hot and loud, a service call for the compressor or charge is warranted.
thread_resolution: the defrost heaters are not turning off — a stuck thermal switch or timer keeps them running, which heats the cabinet (top answer, score 4)
grade_reason: The attempt names condenser coils, condenser fan, and the compressor/charge — a different cause class from the thread's top answer — and none of its actions would find a stuck defrost heater.

attempt: A detergent cup that never opens is usually the wax motor (the small cylinder that pops the cup) or a stuck, clogged cup — not the detergent brand. Check the cup for clogs and free movement by hand; if it moves freely but still will not pop during a cycle, the wax motor or its wiring is the fault, and it is a cheap, accessible part on most machines. Hot water and rinse aid will not fix a cup that never opens.
thread_resolution: the detergent cup's cover is not opening: the solenoid that pulls the catch fails and needs replacement (accepted answer, score 8; confirmed by score 4)
grade_reason: The attempt names the pop mechanism (wax motor / solenoid — the same component class) and the cup-stuck alternative, with the free-movement test the thread's description implies.

attempt: The evidence in the question points to a ground fault from moisture: the ground wire reading 'all over the place' to the frame means damaged insulation or a chafed wire, and it began at defrost, when water enters connections. Leave the machine off and open for 24 hours to dry fully, then re-test. Inspect the ground wire's insulation and any wire routing near the frame or compressor for chafing, and ohm each wire to the frame one at a time. A machine that trips only when the ground is connected has a wire-to-frame fault and should not run until it is found.
thread_resolution: a ground fault: a short between hot and ground somewhere between the plug and the compressor — possibly the receptacle itself (top answer, score 1); a defrost-element oxidation ground fault appears in a lower answer
grade_reason: The attempt's cause class (wire-to-ground fault from damaged insulation, beginning at defrost) matches the thread's, and its actions (dry fully, inspect insulation, ohm each wire to the frame) would find the fault the thread describes.

attempt: Agitates but will not spin, with the coupler, pump, and lid switch verified, points to the clutch and brake assembly (the clutch engages spin only after the timer advances) or the timer never reaching spin. First confirm the timer actually advances to the spin position; if it does and the tub still does not spin, the clutch or brake is the fault — a common wear item on the Kenmore 80 series. The agitator being stoppable by hand during spin is consistent with the transmission not engaging spin.
thread_resolution: examine how the agitator attaches to the drive shaft — it is slipping, or the clutch is slipping (top answer, score 2); a rubber-band return in the drain/spin switch also fails (score 1)
grade_reason: The attempt names the clutch (in the thread's top answer) and the timer-advance check, with a diagnostic path consistent with the thread's reasoning. The agitator-slip and rubber-band causes are not named.

attempt: A microwave that trips the breaker exactly when the door opens mid-heat points to a door interlock switch arcing or shorting as it changes state, or a grounding fault in the door harness. Stop using it, check the door hooks and the door's alignment against the switch actuators (a misaligned door makes a switch bounce), and expect to replace the interlock switches. Do not run it with a door switch defeated.
thread_resolution: the door interlock switches: a sagging door changes the microswitch sequence and trips the breaker (top answer, score 14); a switch shorting to frame on door-open (score 10); the asker's follow-up confirms it was the switches' timing — primary and secondary must open top-first
grade_reason: The attempt names the interlock-switch class and the door-alignment/actuator cause, matching the thread's convergence and its confirmed resolution, with the stop-using-it safety action.

attempt: A power cord that warms near the plug end and is more pliable there localizes the fault: a damaged cord at the strain relief, or a loose or corroded plug-to-outlet contact. Stop using it, check the cord entry for a cracked strain relief and the prongs for corrosion, and feel whether the outlet itself is warm (a worn outlet is the other cause). A heater draws its full load, so a poor connection heats up; the cord or the outlet must be replaced before use.
thread_resolution: the plug is not making good connection at the outlet — a high-resistance connection that heats (top answer, score 1); hotspots are very bad, replacement plugs cost about $4
grade_reason: The attempt's cause class (loose/corroded plug-to-outlet contact, damaged cord at the strain relief) matches the thread's top answer, and its actions (check prongs, feel the outlet, replace the cord or outlet) are the thread's fixes.

attempt: On many stoves the igniters share one ignition module wired so that all of them spark while any burner calls for ignition, so all five sparking while one lights is typical behavior — the abnormal version is sparking that continues after the burner lights. Watch whether the sparking stops the moment the burner catches: if it stops and the burner lights reliably, this is normal; if it continues, one igniter's switch is shorted and should be replaced.
thread_resolution: yes — typical for gas stovetops without a standing pilot: all igniters fire in parallel from one module to reduce complexity (accepted answer, score 9; explained independently at scores 3 and 1)
grade_reason: The attempt states the thread's resolution — shared ignition module, typical behavior — plus the abnormal variant (sparking that continues after lighting) that the thread's answers imply is the failure mode.

attempt: A smell that appears only in fan mode after cooling, fades in about two minutes, and disappears when cooling resumes is the evaporator: in AC mode the coil is cold and dry; in fan mode it warms, and the moisture on it mildews or the condensate pan sours. Run fan mode with the vent open to dry the coil, clean the filter and the condensate pan, and confirm the condensate is draining (portable units either evaporate it or need a drain). A smell that returns within a day means the pan or coil needs a cleaner.
thread_resolution: the evaporator and condensate: brush the coils, clean the evaporation tank/pan, and confirm the condensate drains (top answer, score 1); spores/bacteria on the evap coils (score 0); a comment warns a burnt-winding smell could be a motor meltdown
grade_reason: The attempt names the evaporator/pan class the thread converges on, with the dry-the-coil and clean-the-pan actions the thread's answers give.

attempt: A gas oven that shuts off shortly after preheat and reignites when the surface burners are clicked points to a weak igniter: it glows but does not draw enough current to hold the gas valve open, so the valve closes; clicking a burner resets the circuit. Watch the igniter during the failure — a dull orange glow instead of bright white confirms it. The igniter is a cheap, common part; the gas valve and thermostat are the next suspects if the igniter glows brightly.
thread_resolution: the igniter: the asker's follow-up comment records that a technician replaced the igniter and the oven worked — matching the accepted answer's hypothesis (score 1)
grade_reason: The attempt's primary hypothesis is the weak igniter (glows but cannot hold the valve open), with the watch-the-glow test the thread implies — the thread's confirmed resolution.

attempt: One burner stuck at medium-high regardless of the knob is the burner's infinite switch: a failed switch can feed continuous partial power to that one burner. Turn the breaker off and inspect the switch wiring for a short; the switch itself is the part to replace, and it must match the burner's wattage. If the burner stays hot with the knob off, the switch is welded or shorted and must be replaced before further use.
thread_resolution: the surface element controller has failed; replace it (accepted answer, score 4, confirmed by the comments' part numbers)
grade_reason: The attempt names the same component (infinite switch / surface element controller) and the same action — replace it, matched to the burner's wattage.

attempt: A dryer that spins but never heats, with the timed-dry knob advancing but auto-dry not, points to the heating circuit: the thermal fuse first (the #1 cause of spins-but-no-heat; it sits on the blower housing and kills heat while leaving the motor running), then the heating element and the thermostats; auto-dry not advancing adds the moisture sensor to the list. Test the thermal fuse for continuity, then the element and each thermostat, and check the sensor contacts.
thread_resolution: the heating element had a break on its hidden back side — found by resistance testing and replaced (accepted answer, score 0, the asker's own follow-up); an in-line thermal protection device is the other named cause (score 2)
grade_reason: The attempt names the thermal fuse first (the standard #1 cause) and the heating element second with the continuity test that is exactly how the thread's resolution was found.

attempt: A dishwasher that fills, heats, and drains while the wash pump never runs — relay clicks, no hum, no fault codes — points to the pump motor, the relay or control board driving it, or the wiring to the pump: the control thinks it ran. With power off, check the pump connector for corrosion and the pump motor for continuity; an open motor means a pump replacement, a good motor means the relay or board. The clicking relay with a dead motor is the key symptom.
thread_resolution: test the pump motor's own leads for continuity — 25 megohms through the motor in the asker's follow-up: the motor is shot (accepted answer, score 2, names the correct wires)
grade_reason: The attempt names the pump motor, its drive relay/board, and the wiring, and prescribes the continuity test on the pump motor that the thread's resolution used.

attempt: Both elements dead with controls and light working is almost never two elements at once: it is a lost 240 V leg (120 V still runs controls and lights but heats nothing), a failed oven relay on the control board, or the elements' wiring. Check the breaker (a half-tripped breaker kills one leg) and measure the outlet voltage (200-240 V). If voltage is right, an appliance tech should check the relay and element wiring; if a leg is dead, an electrician is the right call. The diagnosis is knowledge; the fix is a part or a circuit repair.
thread_resolution: check the circuit breaker first (flip off and on), then route the call: an electrician or a large appliance repair shop (accepted answer, score 5; score 4 names the repair shop); the asker's follow-up: the elements and the probe tested fine, and the service sticker inside the drawer was used
grade_reason: The attempt names the breaker check (the thread's first action) and the lost-240V-leg differential that the follow-up's good-elements result is consistent with, and routes to the same two trades the thread names.

attempt: A thermal fuse that blows every few months with a clear exhaust and a good element points to what the fuse is protecting against: on an outdoor dryer, ambient heat and lint ingress, or a failing thermistor reading high and driving the heater until the fuse opens. Verify exhaust airflow under load, check the thermistor's resistance against the measured 61-71C, and confirm the machine is rated for outdoor use — an indoor-rated dryer in sun will overheat. The fuse is the messenger, not the fault.
thread_resolution: replace the thermostat next to the fuse — it is reading low or failing intermittently, so the dryer runs hotter than the control allows (accepted answer, score 3: 'the thermostat solved it after I went through about 5 thermal fuses')
grade_reason: The attempt names the sensor-fault class the thread's accepted answer confirms (a temperature sensor driving excess heat) with a resistance check against measured temperature, plus the airflow checks the thread's other answers give. The specific part is the thermostat, not the thermistor the attempt names.

attempt: Error E64 means the control sees an open heater circuit; a dryer that heats fine for ten to twenty minutes and then throws E64 has a connection that opens when hot: a failing heater terminal (thermal expansion breaking a marginal crimp), a cracked element (passes cold, opens hot), or a failing thermal cutout. Check the heater terminals for heat discoloration and retorque them; test the element cold and remember a cracked element can pass cold. Clean connections point to the heater assembly.
thread_resolution: the heating coil had a broken circuit in one of its three legs, found with a multimeter and replaced (the asker's own follow-up, score 1)
grade_reason: The attempt names the cracked-element class (passes cold, opens hot) — the thread's resolution — with the resistance test that found it, and the terminal-connection check the mechanism implies.

attempt: Orange flames with soot on every propane appliance, a backfiring generator, and two regulators already replaced points to the supply itself: bad propane, a still-faulty regulator or second stage, or a leak drawing air into the line. Stop using the appliances (soot means incomplete combustion and a CO risk) and ask the propane company for a gas-quality test, simultaneous pressure readings at every appliance, and a leak-down test with the system pressurized and isolated. Appliance-level fixes cannot address a problem the generator shares.
thread_resolution: insufficient vaporization/pressure: operate one device at a time (score 28) and hold the low-pressure side above 11 inches of water column with all appliances firing — below that, look for an obstruction (accepted answer, score 25, from a propane service technician)
grade_reason: The attempt names bad propane, a faulty regulator, and an air leak — the thread's minority causes — and its actions (gas-quality analysis, leak-down) would not find the vaporization/pressure problem the thread converges on, whose test is a water-column gauge under full load.

attempt: Lights on but no compressor or fan sound at all means the compressor is not starting: the start relay or overload (most common, especially after years in storage), a seized compressor, or rarely a stuck defrost timer. A full condensation tray says it ran and defrosted. Unplug, check the relay on the compressor (a rattling relay has loose guts), and the overload; if the compressor hums but does not start, the compressor may be seized. After long storage, oil settles and relays stick — replace the relay before condemning the compressor.
thread_resolution: a frozen coil from low refrigerant: the asker left it off for a day, the coil thawed, and it worked again; a shirtsleeve diagnosis in the comments ties the full condensation tray to a frozen coil and low Freon
grade_reason: The attempt's cause class (start relay, overload, seized compressor) does not match the thread's converged cause (frozen coil / low refrigerant), and its resolution (thaw, check the charge) is absent.

attempt: A fridge light that only comes on when the freezer door opens means the door-switch wiring is crossed: the freezer switch is wired into the fridge light circuit, or the two switches' leads are swapped. Check the wiring at both door switches against the diagram; this is a wiring job, not a part. If the wiring is correct, one switch's contact is cross-conducting and should be replaced. It is a low-voltage repair once the panel is off.
thread_resolution: a control-board fault: there was an undiscovered third magnetic switch below the fridge door, and pressing buttons on the control board fixed the light (accepted answer, score 2, with the asker's and commenters' follow-ups)
grade_reason: The attempt's crossed-wiring hypothesis was not the cause: the thread's resolution was the control board and an undiscovered switch, neither of which the attempt names.

attempt: Oven bulbs burning out every week or two across several brands points to heat or voltage: a loose socket contact (arcing kills bulbs), a bulb not rated for oven use, or high supply voltage. Check the socket for a loose or corroded contact (wobble the base), confirm replacements are oven-rated (not LED unless the oven says so), and measure the supply voltage at the outlet — over about 125 V kills bulbs. A loose socket contact is the most common cause of rapid bulb death.
thread_resolution: no fault was found: the asker's follow-up (accepted answer, score 4) records the latest bulb lasting 10+ months — a streak of bad bulbs; the comments give the real differential (loose socket, supply voltage, a loose neutral in the panel)
grade_reason: The attempt's differential (socket contact, bulb rating, supply voltage) is the thread's diagnostic path, and its tests would correctly conclude 'no fault' on this machine — which is what the thread found.

attempt: Error 4U00 on a Bosch hob right after wiring means the hob detected an installation fault: the 5-wire connection is wrong (terminal mapping, phase, neutral, or earth), the supply does not match the hob's rating, or a connection is loose or a strand is shorting between terminals. Turn the power off and re-check the wiring terminal-for-terminal against the hob's diagram, confirm the supply voltage and phase arrangement match the rating plate, and inspect for stray strands. The manual's 4U00 entry names the exact fault; a mis-wired terminal is the most common cause.
thread_resolution: the wiring/phase configuration: hobs are mostly single-phase despite the 'three-phase' name — check the terminal mapping against the diagram and the supply against the rating plate (accepted answer, score 7, with the volt-meter and breaker-count checks of scores 4 and 2)
grade_reason: The attempt names the terminal-mapping, phase-arrangement, and supply-matching classes the thread converges on, with the same actions (re-check terminal-for-terminal, confirm supply matches the plate).

attempt: Outlets that die or a breaker that pops when a microwave runs points to an overloaded or damaged circuit: the microwave's 1000-1500 W draw on a shared circuit, or a loose or damaged connection in the flipped house's wiring (a bad neutral is the classic — outlets die and breakers pop under load). Move the microwave to a different circuit and test; check the outlet's wiring (back-stabbed connections are a common failure in flipped houses) and the breaker itself. If it follows the microwave, the microwave is the fault; if it stays on the circuit, the wiring or breaker is.
thread_resolution: an AFCI breaker tripping on a genuine arc fault — poor contacts and back-stabbed connections top the hit-list (top answer, score 3); the comments add undersized wire and shared neutrals

attempt: A breaker that is hot to the touch and pops when the oven calls for full heat is most likely failing itself: a weak contact heats and trips under load, and the stove is probably fine. Have an electrician replace the breaker and check the wire torque at its terminals (a loose wire heats the breaker the same way). If a new breaker still pops at high heat, then the oven's element or wiring is shorting — but a hot breaker is the breaker's own signature.
thread_resolution: a heating element with deteriorated insulation: the magnesium-oxide tube expands when hot and shorts the inner wire to the sheathing — replace the elements (top answer, score 17); a bad breaker is 'less likely'
grade_reason: The attempt's primary (a failing breaker, stove probably fine) is the thread's less-likely cause, and its action (replace the breaker) is not the thread's resolution (replace the elements).

attempt: Hollow, shell-like ice cubes are the signature of low water pressure to the ice maker or a faulty water inlet valve: the mold does not fill before the freeze cycle ends. Check the supply valve is fully open and the line is not kinked, and clear the inlet valve's screen; if a sink tap on the same line runs weakly, house pressure is the cause. If pressure is good at a tap, the inlet valve is the likely fault. A too-warm fridge or a mis-level fridge can also make hollow ice, but pressure is the first check.
thread_resolution: insufficient water flow to the ice maker: the clamp-on saddle valve was the restriction; soldering in a 1/4-inch brass line with a proper shut-off valve fixed it permanently (top answer, score 4)
grade_reason: The attempt's primary class (low water pressure/flow to the ice maker) and its supply-side checks (valve open, line not kinked, weak tap flow on the same line) are the thread's resolution class — the saddle valve is a supply restriction.
